vignette:
He is 25, European, and works as a salesperson, but the life he describes feels divided into “before” and “after” the war. Before the fighting reaches his city, he is building a routine he likes: waking early, dressing carefully, and spending most of his day talking to customers, reading their mood quickly, and adjusting his tone until they trust him. He enjoys the rhythm of sales, the way a conversation can be turned, the small satisfaction of closing a deal. He is in a relationship, and at that time he imagines his life moving in a fairly ordinary direction.

Then the war arrives, first as a distant tension and then as something immediate and unavoidable. He remembers the first explosions as unreal, like thunder with no storm. Soon the streets he knows become dangerous to cross, sirens interrupt every thought, and his phone fills with messages about where to find shelter and which roads are still open. He tries to keep working at first, partly because he needs the money and partly because routine feels like a handhold. He takes calls from home when he can, speaking in the same polished, reassuring voice he uses with customers, but now he is selling calm he does not feel. He says it becomes harder to focus on a product when he is listening for air-raid alarms.

The worst moments come when he leaves the apartment and cannot predict whether he will get back. He describes walking with his shoulders tight, scanning rooftops and intersections without meaning to, already bracing for the sound he dreads. He learns the geography of danger quickly: which streets are exposed, which buildings have basements, which silence is suspicious. He has an image of himself as someone who is always calculating exits. Even now, he does not like sitting with his back to a door. He does not like crowds, because they feel unstructured and impossible to monitor. He notices every loud engine, every sudden bang, every helicopter overhead, and his body reacts before his mind can settle the question of whether he is safe.

At one point he witnesses destruction close enough to feel personal rather than abstract. He does not describe it theatrically; instead, he speaks in a controlled voice that tightens when he reaches the details. He remembers dust in his mouth, people shouting, the stunned feeling of moving through a scene that no longer obeys ordinary rules. Afterward, he begins to carry the event in fragments: a sound, a smell, the color of smoke against a gray sky. These fragments come back without warning. He is startled by slamming doors and by the sharp crack of a dropped object. At night he wakes already tense, before he can remember what has happened, and then the memories rush in and make sleep feel unreliable.

Even in a safer place now, his mind does not fully accept that the danger has ended. He checks windows and locks more than once. He prefers sitting where he can see the room, and in public he watches other people’s hands as much as their faces. He says he is tired in a way that rest does not fix. When he drives or hears certain sounds, his thoughts race ahead to worst-case scenarios, and he has to make a conscious effort to come back to the present. Sometimes he feels detached from the people around him, as if part of him remains in the war zone and part of him is going through the motions elsewhere. His partner notices that he is more irritable and less easy to reach. He hates this change in himself, which only increases the distance.

At work, he is still capable and careful, but the old ease is gone. He can still persuade people, yet he feels drained after simple conversations. If a customer raises their voice, even in ordinary frustration, he feels a jolt of anger and alarm that is out of proportion to the moment. He works hard to look composed. This matters to him because his job depends on confidence, eye contact, and control, and because he does not want the war to become the most visible thing about him. Still, he finds himself distracted, rehearsing safety plans even when he is supposed to be listening to a client.

He presents as someone who has learned to keep functioning while carrying too much inside. He continues to love his partner, continues to work, continues to show up, but everything is filtered through alertness. The war has ended for the outside world in ways that do not always reach him, and he lives with the sense that one wrong sound, one unexpected shift, could bring it all back.
